chunks.content: Nadodrze is a Wrocław osiedle (settlement/district) carved out of Ołbin in 1991, north of the Old Town. Its territory, historically called 'Przedmieście Odrzańskie' (German: Oder Vorstadt), was incorporated into the city in 1808 after the demolition of the city fortifications. Population ~22,259 (2024). It survived WWII with relatively little damage, becoming the 'temporary city centre' in the first post-war years: in mid-April 1945 the Polish administration around Bolesław Drobner, the first post-war president of Wrocław, set up its temporary seat at today's ul. Poniatowskiego 25/27. The district contains Kępa Mieszczańska island, the Wrocław Nadodrze railway station, tram depot no. 2 on ul. Słowiańska, and the Wrocław power plant. The Nadodrze Council sits at ul. Rydygiera 43; the 'Łokietka 5 – Infopunkt Nadodrze' supports local community and cultural initiatives.

Nadodrze is a Wrocław osiedle (settlement) carved out of Ołbin in 1991, north of the Old Town. Its territory, historically called 'Przedmieście Odrzańskie' (German: Oder Vorstadt), was incorporated into the city in 1808 after the demolition of the city fortifications. Population ~22,259 (2024). It survived WWII with relatively little damage, becoming the 'temporary city centre' in the first post-war years: in mid-April 1945 the Polish administration around Bolesław Drobner, the first post-war president of Wrocław, set up its temporary seat at today's ul. Poniatowskiego 25/27. The district contains Kępa Mieszczańska island, the Wrocław Nadodrze railway station, tram depot no. 2 on ul. Słowiańska, and the Wrocław power plant. The Nadodrze Council sits at ul. Rydygiera 43; the 'Łokietka 5 – Infopunkt Nadodrze' supports local community and cultural initiatives.

Nadodrze is known for monumental tenement houses (kamienice) from the turn of the 19th/20th centuries along main arteries such as ul. Bolesława Chrobrego and ul. Jedności Narodowej, hidden courtyards ('studnie') behind large wooden gates, and a thriving street-art scene. Once a working-class and craftsman district, it is considered one of the most valuable enclaves of 19th-century residential architecture in Wrocław. Revitalisation since 2010 has cost over 140 million PLN (about 40 million from EU funds), covering tenement renovations, courtyards, greenery, schools and premises let to galleries, studios and craft workshops — though gentrification tensions remain. Murals cluster around pl. Staszica and ul. Księcia Witolda; murals on ul. Rydygiera reference the industrial past. A further courtyard renewal (block bounded by Kilińskiego, Jedności Narodowej, Poniatowskiego and Prusa, ~10,000 m², formerly home to a pre-war sausage factory, the post-war 'Pionier' cinema, a tool factory and a hospital on Poniatowskiego) is planned to start in 2027. Visitors are advised to explore on foot in morning light and respect residents' privacy in the courtyards.

Wrocław Nadodrze station, at pl. Staszica 50 / pl. Powstańców Wielkopolskich, opened 28 May 1868 as the second-to-last standard-gauge station built in Wrocław, designed by Hermann Grapow (often confused with Wilhelm Grapow). Built of unplastered red brick, about 190 m long, in historicist styles of 1860s Germany; three storeys with three projections, the central one four storeys with an arched portico; listed as a monument (reg. A/2500/344/Wm, 1977). Originally called Rechte-Oder-Ufer-Thorbahnhof, later Breslau Odertor; it was the first station of the Right-Bank Oder Railway, serving the line to Oleśnica and Fosowskie (line no. 143), expanded until 1912. In July 1945 it was the first central Wrocław station to resume service (trains to Kraków, Warsaw, Szczecin), and the city's first post-war tram line no. 1 connected it with Biskupin. Until 1950 a nearby narrow-gauge station (Wrocław Wąskotorowy) linked to Trzebnica. The building was transferred from PKP in 2009 to the Voivodeship Marshal's Office, then to Polregio; since 2022 the owner is DL Invest Group, which plans modernisation with office, dining and retail uses. The station building was closed in March 2020 and remained shut with interiors in poor condition; the station still serves ~1,700 passengers (2024) on the Dolnośląska Kolej Aglomeracyjna, and pl. Staszica in front hosts a secondary bus hub.

The 'Kolorowe Podwórka' (Colourful Courtyards) on Nadodrze are courtyards inside the block bounded by ul. Roosevelta, Henryka Brodatego and Jedności Narodowej — a free open-air gallery of over 3,000 m² of wall paintings, ceramic reliefs and sculptures. Initiated in 2013 by painter Mariusz Mikołajek with Witold Liszkowski, Jan Mikołajek and the OKAP (Ośrodek Kulturalnej Animacji Podwórkowej) team, starting with portraits of residents; in 2014–2017 two thematic areas were created ('Podwórko – nasze atelier' and 'Podwórko – odkrywanie sztuki'). A courtyard Guest Book has been kept since 2016. The project is co-financed by the City of Wrocław and is considered one of the most remarkable public-art projects in the city; a second colourful courtyard at Roosevelta 5A features residents' portraits, a paradise garden and animals.

Ulica Bolesława Chrobrego is one of Nadodrze's main arteries, lined with monumental turn-of-the-19th/20th-century tenement houses. Historic photos show that some pre-war kamienice on the street no longer exist — a primary school (SP nr 108) now stands on the site of demolished tenements. The street retains original pre-war urban fabric, as Nadodrze survived the war far better than the Old Town.

sources.title: Nadodrze — przewodnik po najciekawszej dzielnicy Wrocławia
sources.snippet: Aug 19, 2026 · Nadodrze to najbardziej niejednoznaczna dzielnica Wrocławia — odnowione kamienice obok zaniedbanych podwórek, pracownie artystów obok starych zakładów. Zobacz, co obejrzeć podczas spaceru, co dała rewitalizacja za ponad 140 mln zł i jak naprawdę się tu mieszka.
